content: Detailed searches for articles can be conducted using PubMed (the Medline database) or by visiting the websites of individual publishers. To search via PubMed, users can select the option Search for articles through PubMed (Medline) and then choose between two methods: retrieving citations for all articles on a specific subject (some of which may not be available online or accessible to HINARI users) or retrieving citations only for articles accessible through HINARI. The menu page provides links to regional journal indexes, including the African Index Medicus (AIM), the Index Medicus for the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region (IMEMR), the Latin American and Caribbean Center on Health Sciences Information (LILACS), and the Index Medicus for the South-East Asia Region (IMSEAR). Users can click on these links for direct access to index information. Links to full-text reference sources are available, including databases, encyclopedias, books, and other resources. Additionally, links to free journal collections are provided, such as BioMed Central, Free Medical Journals, Free Books for Doctors, PubMed Central, and SciELO. Institutions eligible for HINARI access, such as academic, government, or research organizations in qualifying countries, can register by completing a registration form. Once registered, a common username and password will be issued for all staff at the institution. It is recommended that the institution's librarian serve as the primary contact point. As of February 2004, eligible countries in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region include Afghanistan, Djibouti, Iraq, Jordan, Morocco, Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, Tunisia, West Bank and Gaza, and Yemen. Various bibliographic and research tools are available, such as CDMARC Bibliographic Library of Congress, the CD-ROM Directory (which provides details on commercially available CD-ROM titles), and computer-related databases. Specific databases include EMBASE, which contains over 1,300,000 abstracts and citations from the past decade, focusing on drugs, pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and adverse drug reactions. Other databases include ERIC (Educational Resources Information Centre), ExtraMED (covering over 220 biomedical journals, primarily from developing countries), and Food and Human Nutrition (with an international perspective and over 135 participating countries). MEDLINE encompasses information from Index Medicus, Index to Dental Literature, and the International Nursing Index, along with additional unpublished data. Other resources include the Oxford English Dictionary (Second Edition) on Compact Disc, POPLINE (a bibliographic database with over 150,000 citations on population and family planning), and Ulrich’s International Periodicals Directory. Guidelines for writing references for scientific papers are based on the Uniform Requirements for Manuscripts submitted to Biomedical Journals, issued by the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. This style, known as the Vancouver style, is largely based on an ANSI standard adapted by the National Library of Medicine (NLM). Authors should follow the specific style guidelines of the journal to which they are submitting their paper. For journal articles, standard citation formats include listing the first six authors followed by et al. if there are more than six authors. For books, the format varies depending on whether the author is an individual, an editor, or an organization. Chapters in books, conference proceedings, and unpublished materials also have specific citation formats. Electronic materials, such as journal articles in electronic format or monographs on CD-ROM, require additional details like the medium and access date. Most medical journals use the Vancouver system, where references are numbered in the order they are cited in the text. Some journals use the Harvard system, which identifies references by author name and publication year. Early drafts of manuscripts may benefit from using the Harvard system to avoid renumbering references during revisions. The Bangkok Declaration on Health Research for Development emphasizes that health is a fundamental human right and that health research is essential for improving health, social, and economic development. The declaration highlights the importance of addressing social and gender equity, ensuring publicly funded research is accessible to all, and recognizing research as an investment in human development. It calls for effective governance, coordinated strategies, and partnerships to address global health disparities and improve decision-making through high-quality evidence. The glossary of health research terms includes definitions for key concepts such as abstracts, action research, adjusted rates, analytical studies, alternative hypotheses, anonymous linked information, assignment methods, attributable risk, and baseline phases in intervention studies. These terms are essential for understanding and conducting health research effectively.
